On returns, it claims: “In 2026, the average payback period is around 7 to 10 years,” and says a “£5,000 5kWh system could save a household around £500 to £800 a year,” especially when stored solar energy is used in the evening. It separately says that a 10kWh battery might save £700–£900 annually in brighter parts of Southern England, but these statements are explicitly framed around storing solar energy and therefore are not evidence for battery-only arbitrage.
findings.summary: The webpage supports using approximately £3,200–£4,200 for a 5 kWh installed system and £4,600–£7,100 for a 10 kWh system as preliminary quotation ranges, with LFP efficiency and usable-capacity assumptions broadly around 92–98% and 90–100% respectively. It also suggests that 0% VAT may apply to qualifying installations until 2027, subject to the precise tax rules and installation configuration. It does not establish that either battery size will pay for itself without solar: its advertised £500–£800 annual savings and 7–10-year payback are solar-oriented and cannot be transferred to a battery charged from the grid. For the stated high-daytime-use household, a battery-only system may have limited cycling because much electricity is consumed during working hours rather than during the evening peak; a tariff change without a battery may therefore be the lower-cost first step. A proper comparison requires half-hourly smart-meter data, the exact import prices and standing charges on candidate time-of-use tariffs, battery usable capacity and power limits, round-trip efficiency, warranty throughput and end-of-warranty capacity, installation quotations, and confirmation of VAT treatment. The strongest conclusion supported by this page is that battery prices are material and that marketing payback claims should be treated cautiously when the proposed system has no solar input.

findings.title: Intelligent Octopus Go | UK's favourite EV tariff | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant to the tariff-without-solar and battery-arbitrage comparison because it describes a smart-meter time-of-use tariff with a six-hour overnight cheap period, an advertised minimum rate of 8p/kWh, and a July 2026 average price-cap rate of 26.11p/kWh. However, it is an EV-specific product page and does not provide battery eligibility, battery charging rules, installation prices, usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, degradation, warranties, or replacement costs. It therefore supplies evidence about a possible tariff and its stated rates, but not enough evidence to calculate a reliable 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery payback.
findings.evidence:
Relevant tariff description: “Automatic smart charging for eligible cars at super low rates + 6h cheap home energy every night = a win for your wallet and your wheels”. The page states: “Smart charge eligible cars from only 8p/kWh” and “Get 6 hours of smart charging for just 8p/kWh plus six hours every night between 11:30pm and 05:30am for your home. Get a quote for your day rate below.” It also states that the tariff depends on a smart meter: “Intelligent Octopus Go is reliant on the UK's smart meter network”.

The page gives the relevant comparison rate for July 2026: “The average electricity unit rate of a standard variable tariff, based on the July 2026 Ofgem energy price cap for customers paying by direct debit, is 26.11p/kWh.” It explains that the advertised saving is only a unit-rate comparison: “Please note that savings apply to unit rates only and exclude standing charges. Standard variable rates vary by region, so your actual percentage saving may vary depending on where you live.”

The page describes how the cheap periods are allocated: “Plug in your car, tell us what time you need your car by and how much charge you need. Then, across all the hours you’re plugged in, we’ll charge your car when energy is expected to be cheaper and often greener and charge you the off-peak rate for up to 6 hours a day.” It further says: “If you need to charge your car immediately, use the ‘bump charge’ button. Bump charges will be charged at your Intelligent Octopus Go day rate”. The page claims: “Over the last year (May 2025 to April 2026), customers on this fixed Intelligent Octopus Go tariff typically saved £771 compared to our standard variable tariff, Flexible Octopus.” It qualifies this claim by saying: “Savings for individual homes vary based on how much electricity you use for your house and EV, and how much you shift towards off-peak hours. Get a quote to compare your rates.”

For the requested household, the page supports only an indicative tariff-only calculation. If 26.11p/kWh is used as the flat-rate comparator and 8p/kWh as the off-peak rate, the gross unit-price spread is 18.11p/kWh before standing charges, losses, and any day-rate premium. At 9,000 kWh/year, paying 26.11p/kWh would cost approximately £2,350/year before standing charge. If all 9,000 kWh could genuinely be supplied at 8p/kWh, the energy cost would be £720/year and the theoretical maximum saving would be approximately £1,630/year; this is not realistic for the stated daytime-heavy household because the page does not establish that ordinary household loads can receive the 8p rate, and it says the product is designed around an eligible car or charger. A battery calculation must additionally use the actual quoted day rate, standing charge, battery round-trip efficiency, usable capacity, maximum power, cycling frequency, degradation, installation cost, and replacement risk. Those data are absent from this webpage.
findings.summary: The strongest usable evidence is that Octopus advertises six hours from 23:30 to 05:30 at 8p/kWh, while the July 2026 average price-cap unit rate is 26.11p/kWh; both rates exclude standing charges and actual rates vary by region. This indicates that changing to a suitable time-of-use tariff could produce meaningful savings if the household can shift substantial consumption overnight. The household’s high daytime office demand and limited manual shifting reduce the likely tariff-only saving, and a battery could shift some overnight energy into daytime use, but this page does not establish that Intelligent Octopus Go permits or economically supports home-battery charging without an eligible EV/charger. It provides no evidence to conclude that either a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery will pay for itself. Before deciding, obtain the supplier’s written tariff terms and personalised day/night rates, half-hourly smart-meter consumption data, and at least several itemised battery quotations covering usable capacity, power limits, efficiency, warranty throughput, degradation, maintenance, backup functionality, VAT, and replacement assumptions.

findings.title: Octopus Go | Off Peak EV Charging for Any Car & Charger | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant mainly because it describes Octopus Go as a smart time-of-use tariff with a five-hour overnight off-peak period, and it confirms that a compatible smart meter is required. These details bear directly on whether the household could charge a battery overnight and reduce peak-period electricity costs. However, the page is specifically aimed at customers with an electric car, does not provide actual regional tariff rates, and supplies no battery prices, technical specifications, consumption-profile data, degradation assumptions, or evidence about battery economics. It therefore supports assessing tariff eligibility and the basic charging window, but it is insufficient by itself to calculate whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery would pay for itself.
findings.evidence:
“Octopus Go. The energy tariff that puts you in control.” The page describes it as “The smart tariff with super cheap electricity between 00:30 - 05:30 every night”. It also states: “Save with low night rates for your home and when fuelling your car.” This indicates a five-hour overnight charging window that could potentially be used to charge a home battery and supply electricity later in the day, subject to the battery's charging rate and usable capacity.

Eligibility requirements include: “Be an Octopus Energy customer”; “Have an electric car that you charge at home”; and “Have a smart meter we can connect to”. The page adds: “You don't need a home EV charger to join Octopus Go.” For meter compatibility, it says: “We can connect to second generation (SMETS2) meters, and some types of first generation (SMETS1) smart meters,” specifically noting that a Secure-branded SMETS1 meter should be connectable. It also says connection generally takes “around 14 days” and requires acceptance of the tariff terms after Octopus is receiving half-hourly readings.

The page warns: “Energy prices are particularly volatile right now, so we're only offering fixed rates at the moment.” It provides a postcode-based “Check your rates” function rather than publishing a generally applicable price. It claims: “Intelligent Octopus Go is the next generation of charging” and offers “super cheap electricity” while claiming customers can “save 69% vs a standard tariff”; this claim is presented in the context of intelligent electric-vehicle charging and is not evidence of a home-battery saving rate. The page also says that customers with solar panels can pair Go only with “certain export tariffs,” although solar is outside the stated assessment scenario.
findings.summary: The source supports only a preliminary tariff conclusion: a smart meter is necessary, Octopus Go has an overnight 00:30–05:30 off-peak period, and the tariff is primarily designed for home EV charging and may require an electric car. Because the household has a smart meter but no stated EV, eligibility must be confirmed with Octopus before using this tariff in the comparison. The webpage does not disclose the actual peak and off-peak prices, standing charge, battery-compatible terms, or future rates, so it cannot establish annual costs, battery savings, payback, or a 10-year net outcome. To complete the requested assessment, obtain a postcode-specific tariff quote and terms, half-hourly household consumption data, and independent installed quotations for 5 kWh and 10 kWh batteries including usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, round-trip efficiency, warranty, degradation, replacement, maintenance, and export or grid-charging restrictions.

findings.title: Export at Octopus Energy | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is only partially relevant to the research goal. It describes Octopus export tariffs for homes with solar, a solar-and-battery tariff, and the combined price of one solar-plus-battery installation. It does not provide the import time-of-use rates, battery-only installation prices, usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, degradation assumptions, warranties, or operating rules needed to assess a battery without solar in England. Consequently, it cannot support reliable annual-cost, payback, or 10-year net-outcome calculations for the four options requested.
findings.evidence:
The page separates its products according to whether the customer has solar: “If you have solar but no home battery or want to combine solar with EV charging” followed by “Agile Outgoing Octopus”, which “Matches your half-hourly prices with day-ahead wholesale rates”; “Outgoing Octopus”, described as a “Variable tariff currently paying a flat rate of 12p/kWh”; and “Smart Export Guarantee (SEG)”, which “offers a flat 4.1p kWh rate for each exported unit of energy and can be combined with an import tariff by any other supplier.”

It then states: “If you have solar and a home battery” and lists “Octopus Flux”, described as “An import and export tariff. Schedule your home battery to get the best rates for consuming and selling your energy during peak periods.” It also lists “Intelligent Octopus Flux”, which “pairs with your battery to optimise your charging and discharging to save you money and help balance the grid” and “Works with GivEnergy, Tesla, SolarEdge and Enphase batteries.” These are export-oriented products and the page does not establish that they are available to a household with a battery but no solar.

Under “If you don't have solar yet”, the page offers “Solar Panel Installation” and says Octopus has engineers “installing solar panels and batteries on domestic properties.” Its quoted price is for a combined solar system: “Our most popular system is a 12 panel installation with a 10kWh smart battery which costs £11,115. All costs are based on April 2026 prices.” It also says: “Your solar and battery system could pay for itself in 9-13 years” and attributes this to the Energy Saving Trust, adding that payback depends on location, time spent at home, electricity use, roof size and orientation, and whether the system includes a battery. This is not a quoted price or payback period for a battery-only installation. The page gives no 5kWh battery price, no battery-only quotation, no flat-rate or import time-of-use tariff prices, and no technical or lifecycle data.
findings.summary: The webpage provides useful evidence that Octopus’s cited Flux and export products are designed around solar generation and export, while its £11,115 figure and 9–13-year payback claim concern a 12-panel solar installation with a 10kWh battery, not a battery-only system. It therefore cannot determine whether a 5kWh or 10kWh battery is worthwhile for the stated high-use, daytime-heavy English household, nor calculate the requested annual costs, savings, payback, or 10-year outcomes. To complete the assessment, the homeowner needs current battery-only installed quotations; usable capacity, power limits, efficiency, degradation and warranty terms; and supplier-confirmed import tariff rates and eligibility for battery-only charging and discharge. The page supplies no evidence that changing tariff without buying a battery would produce meaningful savings, and its solar payback claim should not be transferred to the no-solar case.

findings.title: Octopus Flux | Energy Tariff Designed for Solar & Batteries | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant because it describes Octopus Flux, a time-of-use import/export tariff with cheap overnight charging and expensive evening periods suitable for battery operation. However, it also states that solar panels are mandatory, so Flux cannot be used by the household described unless Octopus changes its eligibility rules. The page provides no actual unit rates, standing charges, battery prices, technical specifications, degradation assumptions, or consumption data, so it cannot support the requested cost, payback, or 10-year financial calculations.
findings.evidence:
Octopus describes Flux as “an import and export tariff optimised to give you the best rates for consuming and selling your energy and support the grid during peak periods.” It states: “Super cheap rates between 02:00 - 05:00 every day, when you can top up your battery with any extra energy you may need. A peak rate between 16:00 - 19:00, the optimum time to discharge your battery and export surplus energy back to the grid.”

The page explicitly limits eligibility: “You need solar panels to be eligible for Octopus Flux, but they don't need to have been installed by us.” It further says applicants need “an Export MPAN” and, under the eligibility requirements, must have “A solar system and home battery” and “Already be on an import and export tariff, both with Octopus Energy.” The page also says that Octopus requires “a copy of the MCS document for your installation before we can complete your switch.”

Flux requires a compatible smart-meter arrangement: customers must have “a smart meter providing us with half-hourly readings.” The page says Flux is a “three rate electricity tariff combining both import and export,” that it is flexible, and that “the unit rate and standing charges can rise and fall with wholesale energy prices.” It also states there are “no exit fees or tie-ins.” Battery control is not automatic by default: “with Octopus Flux you'll need to manually schedule your battery to charge and discharge based on Flux's unit rates,” with the general recommendation to charge from 02:00 to 05:00 and discharge from 16:00 to 19:00. The webpage gives no numerical import prices, export prices, standing charges, installation costs, usable battery capacities, charge/discharge limits, efficiency figures, degradation rates, warranty terms, replacement costs, or evidence about how much of a 9,000 kWh household's demand could be shifted.
findings.summary: This page provides strong evidence that overnight charging and evening discharge are the intended operating pattern, and that a smart meter with half-hourly readings is required. Its most important conclusion for this case is negative: Octopus Flux is explicitly designed for and restricted to customers with both solar and a home battery, so it is not a suitable tariff for evaluating a battery-only installation. The household would need a different battery-compatible time-of-use tariff, and current supplier rates plus an interval consumption profile would be required to compare a flat tariff, tariff-only switching, and 5 kWh versus 10 kWh batteries. The unusually high daytime office demand may reduce battery savings because electricity used during the day cannot generally be shifted from the overnight period unless the battery is large enough and can sustain the relevant daytime load; the source supplies no data to quantify that effect. No defensible annual costs, simple paybacks, 10-year net outcomes, or sensitivity analysis can be calculated from this webpage alone.

findings.title: Intelligent Octopus Flux: Frequently Asked Questions | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The relevant sections explain Intelligent Octopus Flux’s tariff structure, battery-control requirements, eligibility rules, battery operating limits, and Octopus’s April 2026 solar-and-battery pricing. They are directly relevant to assessing whether a battery could save money, but the page is designed for customers with solar panels and does not provide the import rates, standalone battery price, efficiency data, degradation assumptions, or consumption-profile evidence needed for a reliable battery-only calculation.
findings.evidence:
“Intelligent Octopus Flux is a smart import and export tariff optimised to give you the best rates for consuming and selling your energy.” Octopus says that “Import rates on Intelligent Octopus Flux are even lower than Octopus Flux” and that the tariff has “a peak rate between 16:00 - 19:00, where we will export your surplus energy back to the grid.”

The tariff’s charging strategy is described as follows: “Your battery charging is split into 2 parts: Overnight & day time charging. Your battery will charge up using the greenest and cheapest energy - some of this will come from your solar and some from the grid… Afternoon discharge. Your battery will discharge to the grid 4 - 7pm to take advantage of Octopus Flux’s high export rates.” Octopus also states that it controls the battery: “No - once connected we'll take control of scheduling charging and discharging at times that are clean and green.”

The page identifies an important eligibility restriction: customers “need to have: A smart meter providing us with half-hourly readings; A solar system and home battery that we can connect to,” with current integrations listed as “GivEnergy, Enphase, SolarEdge, Tesla.” It further says, “Don't have solar and battery storage yet? We can install a solar system for you.” This indicates that Intelligent Octopus Flux, as described here, is not a battery-only tariff for a home without solar.

Octopus says the tariff is “a variable tariff, which means that the price you pay can rise and fall with the cost of wholesale energy,” while also stating there are “no exit fees or tie-ins.” The page says the battery’s minimum state of charge was “20%” as of 11 October 2023, although this “may vary throughout the year.”

The pricing information is for combined solar-and-battery systems rather than a standalone battery: “Our most popular system is a 12 panel installation with a 10kWh smart battery which costs £11,115. All costs are based on April 2026 prices.” Octopus also says, “Your solar and battery system could pay for itself in 9-13 years,” citing the Energy Saving Trust, but qualifies that payback depends on location, time spent at home, electricity use, roof size and orientation, and whether the system includes a battery. The page gives no price for a roughly 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery installed without solar, and no tariff prices or battery technical specifications from which to calculate annual savings.
findings.summary: This page provides only partial support for the research question. It confirms that a smart meter and half-hourly data are required, that the tariff is variable and has no exit fee, and that Octopus can automate overnight charging and 4–7pm discharge. However, Intelligent Octopus Flux requires a compatible solar system and battery, so it cannot straightforwardly support the no-solar scenario in the question. The quoted £11,115 price is for 12 solar panels plus a 10 kWh battery, not a standalone battery, and the 9–13 year payback claim applies to a complete solar system rather than battery-only storage. Consequently, this webpage cannot establish whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery would pay for itself, calculate annual costs or 10-year outcomes, or assess the effect of the household’s high daytime demand. Further evidence is required: a battery-only installation quotation; current battery usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, warranty and degradation terms; actual half-hourly consumption; and current battery-compatible time-of-use tariffs whose import and peak/off-peak prices can be compared with a competitive flat tariff.

findings.title: Agile Octopus | Half-hourly UK Wholesale Price Tracker | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant to the tariff and operating assumptions in the comparison, particularly whether a smart-metered household can use half-hourly prices and whether batteries are an appropriate way to shift consumption. However, it does not provide the current prices, battery costs, technical specifications, degradation assumptions, or market and tax information needed to calculate reliable annual costs, payback, or 10-year outcomes as of 14 July 2026.
findings.evidence:
The page describes Agile Octopus as “a 100% green electricity tariff with Plunge Pricing” and says it is “directly impacted by wholesale market volatility.” It states: “Agile prices can spike up to 100 p/kWh any time” and that “This tariff is best suited to customers who can shift large amounts of their energy use to avoid these expensive peaks, often by using smart home technologies like solar and batteries.” It also says the tariff is “Perfect for electric vehicles, storage heaters, or anyone who can shift their electricity use outside of peak times.”

The page explains that “With Agile Octopus, you get access to half-hourly energy prices, tied to wholesale prices and updated daily. So when wholesale electricity prices drop, so do your bills – and if you can shift your daily electricity use outside of peak times, you can save even more.” It further states that prices are updated “between 4-8pm every day (usually nearer 4pm)” for the following 24 hours, and that charges are calculated using “the half-hourly data from your smart meter.” A “daily standing charge covers costs including metering, distribution, and other fixed costs.”

The page warns that prices vary substantially: “Price spikes are short-lived, typically lasting 30 minutes to an hour, but they do happen.” Its Price Cap Protect feature “ensures you'll never pay more than 100p / kWh for your electricity, guaranteed.” It also reports that “Between July 2020 and July 2021, unit prices dropped below 2p / kWh 163 times!” and says that during a period of high wholesale prices “it's likely you'll save more money by sticking to a standard variable or fixed tariff throughout the Winter.”

The eligibility requirements are relevant to the stated household: customers must be Octopus customers and have a compatible smart meter. The page says Octopus can connect to “second generation (SMETS2) meters, and some types of first generation (SMETS1) smart meters,” specifically noting that a Secure SMETS1 meter may be compatible. The page also describes automation through an API and IFTTT, including turning devices off when prices are high and operating them when prices are low.

The webpage does not state a current Agile unit-price distribution for 14 July 2026, a representative flat-rate tariff, standing-charge values, export or charging rules, battery installation prices, usable capacities, maximum charge/discharge rates, round-trip efficiency, degradation rates, warranties, replacement costs, maintenance costs, VAT treatment, or any government incentive. It therefore cannot support numerical annual-cost, payback, or 10-year net-present-value calculations for 5 kWh and 10 kWh batteries. It also does not establish how much of this particular household's overnight demand would be consumed directly rather than stored, nor whether its daytime office demand leaves enough evening peak consumption for a battery to discharge on most days.
findings.summary: The source supports a cautious qualitative conclusion: a smart tariff can reduce costs when electricity use is shifted away from expensive periods, but Agile is volatile and is explicitly most suitable for households able to shift substantial demand or automate batteries and other loads. For the described household, whose unusually high office usage occurs mainly during daytime working hours and whose manual load-shifting ability is limited, switching to a time-of-use tariff without a battery may provide only modest or uncertain savings; the result depends on the actual half-hourly profile and tariff. A battery could be financially useful only if it repeatedly charges at sufficiently cheap overnight or low-price periods and discharges during materially more expensive periods, after allowing for losses, degradation, limited power ratings, and capital cost. The webpage provides no evidence to conclude that either a roughly 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery will pay for itself, and no basis for selecting the better size. Before deciding, the homeowner should obtain at least 12 months of half-hourly smart-meter data, current flat and time-of-use tariff quotations including standing charges and all price limits, and itemised installed battery quotations specifying usable capacity, continuous and peak charge/discharge power, round-trip efficiency, warranty and throughput limits, degradation or capacity-retention terms, replacement expectations, maintenance, VAT, and backup-power equipment. The strongest argument against buying the battery on the evidence supplied is that Agile rewards flexible timing, whereas much of this household's demand occurs during working hours and may not coincide with the battery's highest-value discharge period; tariff volatility could also reduce or reverse the expected spread.

findings.title: Outgoing Octopus | Get paid for your solar energy | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant mainly for identifying Octopus export tariffs, smart-meter requirements, tariff compatibility, and the fact that these products are designed principally for homes with solar generation or battery storage. It does not provide the import tariff rates, battery prices, technical specifications, consumption-profile data, degradation assumptions, or regulatory and tax information needed to calculate whether a battery without solar would be financially worthwhile.
findings.evidence:
“Outgoing Octopus | Get paid for your solar energy | Octopus Energy” describes the service as “Perfect for homes with solar panels, battery storage and other types of renewable generation.” It lists three export options: “Agile Outgoing Octopus”—“We match your half-hourly prices, with day-ahead wholesale rates that are uncapped”—and says it is “Best for: those with energy storage who can make the most of dynamic prices, selling electricity when prices are highest and storing it when prices are lowest”; “Outgoing Octopus”—“12p per kWh for every unit you export”; and “Prime Outgoing Octopus”—“Export at prime time (4pm-7pm) for an awesome 16p per kWh and earn a steady 9p per kWh the rest of the day.” The page says Prime Outgoing is “Best for: those with solar and home battery who can easily shift their export to the evening prime when prices are highest.”

The page states that “Outgoing Octopus is a variable tariff. Rates can change, but we'll always give you plenty of notice before they do.” It also says Agile Outgoing and Prime Outgoing are “12 month fixed-term tariff[s] with a locked-in rate formula” and that “There are no exit fees, so you can leave whenever you like.” These statements indicate tariff-price and contract uncertainty, but the page gives no import prices or historic spread suitable for calculating battery savings.

For eligibility, the page says: “You'll need to: 1 Be an Octopus Energy customer”; Octopus initially places a new customer on “one of our standard tariffs”; and “You can only pair Outgoing Octopus with certain import tariffs.” Under “Good to know,” it says: “You'll need a smart meter from which we are able to receive half-hourly export data. This includes almost all SMETS2 meters and most SMETS1 but please contact us for confirmation or if you don't know which one you have.” It also explains that Octopus applies to the DNO for an export MPAN and that the DNO creates the MPAN before the export meter can be enrolled. The page further notes: “If you have started receiving FiT payments in the last 12 months, the FiT rules mean you won't be able to switch to Outgoing Octopus just yet.”
findings.summary: The webpage supports only a narrow part of the assessment. It confirms that Octopus offers export tariffs with 12p/kWh standard export, 16p/kWh from 4pm–7pm and 9p/kWh otherwise on Prime Outgoing, or uncapped half-hourly Agile export pricing, and that a compatible smart meter, Octopus import tariff and export MPAN are required. However, these are export products aimed at solar or other generation; they do not establish the economics of charging a battery from the grid and discharging it to serve the household's own demand. No evidence here supports assumptions about a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery's installed cost, usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, degradation, warranty, replacement, maintenance, import-price spreads, or the household's peak-time usage. Therefore this page alone cannot show annual costs, payback, 10-year net outcome, sensitivity results, or whether either battery size would pay for itself. For the stated no-solar household, the most relevant follow-up evidence would be current import time-of-use tariffs and terms, battery quotations and technical datasheets, and half-hourly consumption data; the export rates matter only if the battery can legally and economically export grid-charged electricity under the selected tariff.

findings.title: Free electricity with Octoplus Saving Sessions | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant to the tariff and demand-shifting aspects of assessing a battery without solar panels: it describes free-electricity sessions, smart-meter eligibility, the timing and unpredictability of sessions, and how Octopus calculates customers’ normal consumption. However, it does not provide battery purchase prices, usable capacity, charge/discharge rates, round-trip efficiency, degradation, warranties, or a standard time-of-use tariff’s rates. It therefore cannot by itself establish whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery would pay for itself.
findings.evidence:
“In these hour-long sessions, the electricity you’d normally use will cost the same, any extra power you use will be free.” The page says sessions are “generally an hour-long slot in the afternoon” and advises customers to shift flexible demand such as “the dishwasher or washing machine,” cooking, EV charging, a heat pump, or an immersion heater into the session. It also states that customers must be Octopus Energy customers signed up to Octoplus, with “a working electric smart meter,” and that joining Free Electricity does not change the customer’s existing tariff: “When you sign up for Free Electricity, you’ll stay on the tariff that you’re on now.”

The page explains that Saving Sessions are based on market conditions: “Because they’re based on dips in the market (which is changing all the time and relatively unpredictable) we don’t know exactly how many opportunities there will be.” It adds that sessions occur when “energy demand is low,” often “in the middle of the work day,” and that customers normally receive notice only the day before because electricity prices are affected by “unpredictable factors like geopolitics and the weather.”

For measurement, Octopus says it uses historical smart-meter readings to determine normal use: “If the Session is on a weekday, we’ll look at your half-hourly usage over the last 10 weekdays. If the Session is at the weekend, we’ll look at your half-hourly usage at that time within the last 4 weekend days. We’ll not include days where a Session took place in these calculations.” The page reports that in 2025 there were “15 sessions, 19 hours worth of free electricity,” but this is a promotional programme result rather than evidence of a predictable annual saving. It provides no information on battery installation costs, battery cycling, losses, degradation, replacement, maintenance, financing, or ordinary time-of-use import-price spreads.
findings.summary: The strongest applicable finding is that a smart-meter customer may obtain some savings without a battery by shifting genuinely flexible consumption into occasional afternoon Free Electricity sessions; this is potentially useful for appliances, but less useful for the household’s daytime home-office demand because that consumption already occurs during the likely session period and may not be shiftable. The programme is uncertain, limited to qualifying Octopus customers, and does not change the underlying tariff. The webpage supplies no evidence needed to calculate annual costs, battery payback, or 10-year net outcomes for the four requested options. A proper comparison would require current flat and time-of-use import rates, half-hourly consumption data, battery quotations, usable capacity, power limits, efficiency, warranty and degradation terms, and assumptions about future tariff spreads and replacement costs.

findings.title: Our Best Tariffs For Electric Cars | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant because it describes a smart time-of-use tariff with overnight electricity pricing, whole-home applicability, smart-meter requirements, tariff variability, and peak/off-peak billing. However, it is specifically an EV-tariff page and does not establish that a household without an EV or compatible charger can join the tariff. It also provides no battery prices, battery technical specifications, degradation assumptions, installation costs, or evidence that the tariff can be used to charge and discharge a standalone home battery.
findings.evidence:
“Our EV tariffs offer cheaper rates at night so you can do all your car charging at lower costs.” The page describes two products: “Intelligent Octopus Go, the UK’s favourite EV tariff where we control your car charging … in exchange for 6 hours at one of the cheapest rates available,” and “Octopus Go, the UK’s original EV tariff … [with] 5 hours of cheap energy every night.”

The page states that whole-home use can receive the off-peak rate: “Does the tariff offer off-peak savings on the whole house? Some providers limit the off-peak rate to just your car. Both of our electric car tariffs let you use off-peak rates for all the energy you use. This is a huge benefit for anyone able to run other energy intensive tasks during off-peak hours.” It further says: “With Intelligent Octopus Go you have access to one of the lowest prices - 11.5p per kWh and from only 8p between 11:30pm - 5:30am for the whole home, plus it smart-charges your car at the cheapest and greenest times overnight.”

The tariff is described as having variable and fixed versions: “Intelligent Octopus Go is offered as a fixed tariff or as a variable tariff, which means that the price you pay can rise and fall with the cost of wholesale energy.” The page also says: “Our variable EV tariffs are covered by the price cap. Our peak and off peak costs are averaged over 24 hours and will come under the current price cap.”

Eligibility is explicitly EV-related. For Intelligent Octopus Go, customers need “a compatible car or charger,” “a smart meter that sends half-hourly readings,” and must be “on supply with Octopus Energy.” For Octopus Go, the page says: “To sign up to Octopus Go you need: To be on supply with Octopus Energy before making the switch. A smart meter we can connect to … An EV and home charger.” It also says that Intelligent Octopus Go requires authorising the app “to control your car or charger.”

The page explains the billing treatment of controlled charging: “All charges managed by Intelligent Octopus Go are charged at off-peak rates - no matter when.” Conversely, “If you need to overwrite Intelligent Octopus Go settings to manually schedule a charge during peak hours, you'll be charged at peak rate.” It says that urgent “boost charges” are billed at the active rate, including “your peak rate for any charging outside” the off-peak period.

The webpage contains inconsistent or context-dependent price references: it mentions “11.5p per kWh,” “8p between 11:30pm - 5:30am,” and later says customers benefit from “a low price night rate of 8p/kWh,” while also stating that “Unit rates vary by region.” It gives no complete peak unit rate or standing charge for the relevant region, stating instead that “Energy rates change by region. You can check what unit rates and standing charge apply in your area on this page.”
findings.summary: This source supports the general proposition that shifting electricity consumption to an overnight time-of-use period could reduce costs, particularly because the stated Intelligent Octopus Go pricing applies to “the whole home” and requires half-hourly smart-meter data. It is potentially relevant to a battery-only strategy if the supplier permits standalone battery charging, but this page does not confirm that: both tariffs are presented as EV tariffs, Octopus Go explicitly requires an EV and home charger, and Intelligent Octopus Go requires a compatible car or charger and supplier-controlled charging. The source therefore cannot support a financial calculation for a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery, nor establish annual savings, payback, degradation, replacement costs, or 10-year returns. It also does not provide the complete regional peak rate, so the tariff spread needed for a battery calculation is missing. Before relying on this tariff, the homeowner should obtain written confirmation from Octopus that a standalone battery is eligible, whether automated battery charging/discharging is permitted, the exact regional peak rate and standing charge, export/import rules, and whether the quoted off-peak rate is current on 14 July 2026.

findings.title: EV charger installation with Octopus Energy: FAQs | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is an Octopus Energy FAQ about EV home-charger installation, not home batteries. It provides limited contextual information relevant to the research goal—namely, that Octopus offers time-based tariffs, requires a smart meter for certain tariffs, and that customers may switch supplier—but it contains no battery prices, battery specifications, electricity-rate spreads, degradation data, or evidence about battery economics. Therefore, it cannot support a reliable comparison of a flat-rate tariff, a time-of-use tariff without a battery, or 5 kWh and 10 kWh home batteries.
findings.evidence:
“Do I have to be an Octopus Energy customer? Nope! Anyone can apply for a charger installation. However you can cut EV charging costs with a tariff like Intelligent Octopus Go, so you might find you want to stick with us afterwards. But this is completely up to you.”

“To take advantage of our Intelligent Octopus Go tariff with cheap overnight charging, you'll need to: Be an Octopus energy customer; Have a SMETS2 smart meter; Have a compatible EV charger or a compatible vehicle.”

The page also states that its EV chargers “all have an output of 7.4kW” and describes an EV charger as a dedicated high-load device. The only government financial support discussed is the EV chargepoint grant: it “covers 75% of the cost of buying and installing an EV charger, up to £500” for eligible renters, plus a workplace-charging scheme. No home-battery grant, VAT treatment, installation price, battery warranty, usable capacity, round-trip efficiency, degradation rate, replacement cost, or maintenance cost is provided.
findings.summary: This source offers only weak background evidence: smart-meter access and supplier eligibility may matter when evaluating time-of-use tariffs, but the cited Intelligent Octopus Go information is specifically for EV charging and does not establish that the tariff is suitable for a battery-only household. The webpage provides no basis for calculating annual costs, savings, payback, 10-year net outcomes, or sensitivity analysis for 6,000, 9,000, or 11,000 kWh of household demand. Additional primary sources are required, including current tariff terms and rates, Ofgem and government rules, manufacturer technical documentation for 5 kWh and 10 kWh batteries, and itemised installed quotations. The unusually high daytime office demand is particularly important because it may reduce the amount of electricity that can be profitably shifted from overnight off-peak periods to peak hours.

Using the stated rates only, replacing electricity priced at £0.247/kWh with 5 hours at £0.095/kWh would save £0.152/kWh for electricity actually moved to that period; 6 hours at £0.08/kWh would save £0.167/kWh. That full-shift assumption is not realistic for this household because much of its office demand occurs during daytime working hours, and the page does not state the peak rates or whether these tariffs are suitable for general-purpose battery charging rather than EV charging.
findings.summary: The strongest relevant finding is that a smart-meter household may access Octopus Go at 9.5p/kWh for five overnight hours or Intelligent Octopus Go at 8p/kWh for six hours, but Intelligent Octopus Go is restricted to specified compatible EV chargers and the page presents both products primarily as EV-charging tariffs. A tariff switch could produce meaningful savings only to the extent that the household can shift consumption into the stated overnight windows; its high daytime office demand reduces that opportunity. The webpage provides no evidence needed to calculate battery economics, including installed cost, usable capacity, round-trip efficiency, power limits, degradation, warranty, replacement, maintenance, peak tariff, or tariff stability. Consequently, it cannot support a conclusion that either a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery will pay back within ten years. Before deciding, the homeowner should obtain the applicable non-EV tariff terms, peak and standing-charge rates, smart-meter eligibility, and at least twelve months of half-hourly consumption data, together with multiple installed battery quotations specifying usable capacity, continuous and peak power, efficiency, warranty, degradation or throughput limits, installation and replacement costs, and backup functionality.

findings.title: FAQs about Octopus Go, the tariff just for EV drivers | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant because it describes Octopus Go, a smart electricity tariff with a five-hour overnight off-peak period, and confirms that electricity used for purposes other than EV charging can receive the low rate. This is relevant to assessing whether a household without solar panels could charge a battery overnight and use stored electricity later. However, the page is an FAQ for EV drivers, was published on 19 March 2019, and does not provide current UK rates, battery prices, battery operating specifications, degradation data, or evidence sufficient to calculate savings as of 14 July 2026.
findings.evidence:
“Can I use my cheap charging period for anything other than charging my car? Of course! During this 5 hour off peak period, any electricity you use will be charged at your low off-peak rate. You can even automate stuff to come on using smart plugs and neat, simple to set up integrations with Alexa and IFTTT – check out some smart home hacks from our brilliant customers.”

“The Octopus Go tariff works with any EV or charger and offers low charging rates within a 5-hour window. Intelligent Octopus Go needs to connect with your car or charger and only works with selected brands. Once connected, Intelligent Octopus Go will automatically charge your EV at the cheapest times of the day.”

“No matter what your IHD says, your off-peak period stays between 00:30 and 05:30.” The page also states that Octopus Go is an electricity tariff and that customers may choose “electricity only” while obtaining gas from another supplier. It mentions that the previously available export arrangements included Outgoing Lite at 8 p/kWh or the Smart Export Guarantee at 4.1p/kWh, but this information is not a current quotation and is not relevant to a no-solar household unless solar generation is later installed.
findings.summary: The source supports one important premise: Octopus Go historically offered a fixed 00:30–05:30, five-hour low-price period, and all household electricity—not only EV charging—could use that rate. A battery could therefore be charged overnight and discharged during expensive periods, subject to its usable capacity, charge/discharge power, losses, and the household's load profile. For the stated home, the high daytime office demand may reduce the battery's opportunity to discharge during peak periods, while some overnight demand would bypass the battery; therefore a full daily cycle cannot be assumed. The webpage contains no current 2026 tariff prices or standing charges, no confirmation that the tariff remains available on the stated terms, and no battery costs or technical evidence. It cannot by itself establish annual costs, payback, 10-year net outcome, sensitivity results, or whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery is worthwhile. Current supplier tariff quotations, interval smart-meter consumption data, and independent or manufacturer battery specifications would be required for those calculations.

findings.title: Intelligent Octopus Flux | Automated export to support the grid | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant because it describes Octopus Energy’s smart time-of-use battery tariff, its charging and discharging periods, smart-meter dependence, and eligibility requirements. However, it is primarily a solar-export product page and does not provide the tariff rates, battery prices, technical specifications, degradation assumptions, or eligibility rules needed to calculate whether a battery without solar would pay for itself.
findings.evidence:
“With solar & storage you could earn up to £300 more than you pay for electricity.”

“Intelligent Octopus Flux pairs with your battery to optimise your charging and discharging to save you money and help balance the grid.”

“We’ll export the energy you have stored when you’ll make the best return. So you’ll always get the best deal on the sunshine you have stored and could even make up to £300/year profit.” This wording indicates that the advertised potential benefit is based on solar and energy export, rather than ordinary household consumption alone.

“You’ll need solar panels to be eligible for Intelligent Flux.” This directly rules out using the advertised Intelligent Octopus Flux product for the stated no-solar household, at least according to this page.

“Intelligent Octopus Flux is reliant on the UK's smart meter network.” The household has a smart meter, so the technical metering prerequisite appears consistent with the product, although the solar requirement remains decisive.

“Important: Energy prices are particularly volatile right now, so this tariff is temporarily unavailable. We’ll update this page as soon as it’s back. But you don’t have to wait to make your solar and battery work harder for you — our standard Octopus Flux tariff is available right now, offering fantastic import and export rates.” This establishes that the intelligent tariff is unavailable at the stated time and that the page does not give fixed rates for either product.

“Import rates even lower than standard Flux, we’ll make sure your battery charges when the grid is the greenest.”

“A peak rate between 16:00 - 19:00, our optimum time to discharge your battery and export surplus energy back to the grid.” The 16:00–19:00 peak period is relevant to modelling a battery, but the page does not state the actual peak or off-peak prices, so the saving per kWh cannot be calculated from this source.

Using only the household assumptions supplied in the research question, the flat-rate comparison is approximately £2,223 per year: 9,000 kWh × £0.247/kWh. The webpage supplies no figures that allow a defensible annual cost for a time-of-use tariff, or a payback calculation for 5 kWh or 10 kWh batteries. It also supplies no installed costs, usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, round-trip efficiency, warranty, degradation, replacement, maintenance, export-metering, tax, or incentive information.
findings.summary: The page provides one strong conclusion: Intelligent Octopus Flux cannot be used as the basis for a no-solar battery case because it explicitly requires solar panels, and it was temporarily unavailable owing to price volatility. It does suggest that a smart tariff can charge a battery cheaply and discharge it during the 16:00–19:00 peak, but it gives no rates or financial assumptions. Therefore, the only supported numerical comparison is the supplied flat-rate baseline of about £2,223 annually for 9,000 kWh. Whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery, or a tariff change without a battery, is worthwhile cannot be established from this webpage; the homeowner would need current no-solar tariff eligibility and prices, half-hourly consumption data, battery quotations, usable-capacity and power specifications, efficiency and degradation warranties, and replacement-cost assumptions. The unusually high daytime office demand may also reduce battery savings because electricity used directly during the day is not available for shifting from overnight off-peak periods.

findings.title: Energy-saving materials and heating equipment (VAT Notice 708/6) - GOV.UK
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant to the tax treatment of installing a home battery in England. It confirms that batteries for storing energy converted from electricity were added to the qualifying energy-saving materials from 1 February 2024, and that qualifying installations in residential accommodation are zero-rated until 31 March 2027. This is an important input to the installed-cost assumption for a battery purchased by 14 July 2026, although the page provides no evidence about battery prices, tariffs, usable capacity, efficiency, degradation, cycling, or expected savings. Therefore, it supports a VAT adjustment but cannot by itself establish whether a battery without solar panels is financially worthwhile.
findings.evidence:
From section 1.1, “This notice explains when the installation of energy-saving materials and heating equipment is zero-rated or reduced-rated.” It states that the notice covers “supplies of installations of energy-saving materials made between 1 May 2023 and 31 March 2027” and that “From 1 April 2027 onwards, supplies of installations of energy-saving materials will revert to the reduced rate of VAT of 5%.”

Section 2.1 states: “A zero rate applies to the installation of certain specified energy-saving materials from 1 May 2023 to 31 March 2027.”

Section 2.3 explains the scope: “The relief applies to the services of installing energy-saving materials in residential accommodation and charitable buildings.” It also says: “The relief also applies to the supply of energy-saving materials by the person who installs those materials in residential accommodation and charitable buildings. For example, where a customer employs a business to supply and install those materials.” However, “if you supply energy-saving materials without installing them your supply will be standard-rated. For example, the sale of energy-saving materials by a retailer is always standard-rated.”

Section 2.7 lists the qualifying materials and says: “From 1 February 2024 additional materials include: water source heat pumps (read section 2.18); batteries for storing energy converted from electricity (read section 2.19); smart diverters (read section 2.20).”
findings.summary: For an English homeowner buying a professionally supplied and installed qualifying home battery on 14 July 2026, the webpage indicates that the battery installation should generally benefit from 0% VAT, provided the contract falls within the stated energy-saving-materials relief. A battery bought separately from a retailer is standard-rated, and installations are scheduled to return to 5% VAT from 1 April 2027. This may reduce the quoted cost and improve payback, but the source contains no information from which to calculate annual electricity costs, tariff savings, simple payback, 10-year net outcome, or comparisons between 5 kWh and 10 kWh batteries. Those calculations require separate evidence on time-of-use tariffs, installation quotations, battery technical limits, losses, degradation, warranties, replacement costs, and the household’s half-hourly demand profile.

findings.title: Powering Up Britain: Net Zero Growth Plan - GOV.UK
findings.rational: The provided GOV.UK webpage is a national policy document about net-zero growth, energy security, investment and the development of low-carbon technologies. It contains only limited, high-level references to electricity storage and future wholesale electricity prices, and does not provide the household-level evidence needed to compare a flat tariff, a time-of-use tariff, or 5 kWh and 10 kWh batteries in England as of 14 July 2026. In particular, it has no battery prices, tariff rates, usable capacities, charge or discharge limits, efficiency figures, degradation assumptions, warranties, replacement costs, or domestic electricity-demand data.
findings.evidence:
“After decades of reliance on imported fossil fuels, the new Department for Energy Security and Net Zero’s mission is to replace them with cheaper, cleaner, domestic sources of energy.”

“Our ambition is to hit our net zero targets while delivering among the cheapest wholesale electricity prices in Europe. This is why the Prime Minister pledged at COP27 to achieve our ambitious net zero commitment and Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), create new high-wage jobs and protect UK energy security.”

“Investment is the key to delivering our energy security, carbon targets and seizing the economic benefits – the jobs, exports, and productivity gains – of the transition. We need investment at scale across a range of sectors to rapidly rollout existing technologies and bring through transformative new technologies. Established technologies, such as offshore wind turbines, need to be constructed at pace to meet our ambitions for decarbonising power and delivering wholesale UK electricity prices that rank among the cheapest in Europe by 2035.”

“This investment has had an impact across renewables, hydrogen, CCUS, nuclear, sustainable materials, energy storage, electrified transport and clean heat.”

“The UKIB expects clean energy to be the largest sector in its portfolio and is building a strong pipeline of opportunities in areas such as hydrogen, CCUS, electricity storage and clean transport.”

The page was published under the 2022 to 2024 Sunak Conservative government and is dated 2023. It therefore cannot establish current tariff prices, installation costs, incentives or market rules for the requested 14 July 2026 assessment.
findings.summary: The source supports only the general proposition that the UK views electricity storage as part of the clean-energy transition and aims to reduce wholesale electricity costs over time. It does not directly answer whether a battery without solar is financially worthwhile for this household, nor does it support indicative annual costs, savings, payback periods, 10-year outcomes, or the requested sensitivity analysis. A valid assessment would require current supplier tariff quotations and the household’s half-hourly smart-meter data, plus manufacturer or installer quotations covering usable capacity, maximum power, round-trip efficiency, degradation, warranty, maintenance and replacement terms. Based on this webpage alone, no defensible comparison can be made between the four options.

findings.title: Warm Homes Plan (HTML) - GOV.UK
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant because it describes the UK government’s planned support for household batteries, flexible electricity tariffs and home-upgrade finance. However, it does not provide the tariff prices, battery specifications, installed costs, degradation assumptions, or household demand-profile data needed to calculate whether a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery without solar would pay for itself in England.
findings.evidence:
Warm Homes Plan, Executive summary: “Solar panels, insulation, batteries, and heat pumps can all save families hundreds of pounds a year.” It adds that the government wants “every household in Britain, regardless of circumstance, to have access to these transformative technologies.”

Warm Homes Plan, Executive summary: “For a homeowner, this means grant support to upgrade to clean heating, or low-cost finance to cover the upfront cost of a solar or battery installation, and the chance to cut their energy costs even further by taking advantage of a new flexible tariff to use energy when it’s cheapest.”

Warm Homes Plan, “Our offer to consumers (Chapter 3)”: “Government finance will come from a new Warm Homes Fund designed to support the entire home upgrade supply chain with loans and investments to bring down costs and scale up deployment of solar panels, batteries, heat pumps and other technologies.” The page says the fund includes “£1.7 billion already allocated to low- and zero-interest consumer loans (supported by £300 million of capital investment)” and that the remaining funding will support “investments in and loans to the home upgrade sector.”

Warm Homes Plan, “How we will deliver at scale (Chapter 4)”: the government intends to provide households with “information, support” and a “reformed system of comprehensive and robust consumer protection.” It also says Distribution Network Operators will be important in managing “millions of homes running on clean, flexible energy.”

The page contains no specific battery purchase or installation prices; no 5 kWh or 10 kWh usable-capacity figures; no maximum charge or discharge rates; no round-trip-efficiency or degradation data; no warranty or replacement assumptions; no electricity supplier tariff names or peak/off-peak prices; no export-payment information; and no evidence about how much electricity a battery-only household can shift when much of its demand occurs during daytime working hours. It also does not state that a grant or loan is universally available to an individual homeowner, nor does it quantify the effect of VAT, other taxes, market charges or tariff restrictions.
findings.summary: This source supports only the general proposition that batteries, flexible tariffs and possible low-cost government finance are part of the Warm Homes Plan. It cannot support the requested annual-cost, payback or 10-year net-outcome calculations for the four options. A defensible comparison would require current supplier quotations for a competitive flat tariff and battery-compatible time-of-use tariffs; half-hourly smart-meter data for at least a full year; the battery’s usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, warranty and degradation schedule; installed-price quotations; financing and grant eligibility; maintenance and replacement costs; and confirmation of the applicable VAT and electricity-market rules. Based on this webpage alone, no conclusion can be drawn about whether either battery size will pay for itself, whether tariff switching alone will produce meaningful savings, or which option offers the best financial outcome.

findings.title: Ofgem's energy price cap explained - Energy Saving Trust
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant to establishing the England electricity-price context for the assessment date: it gives the July–September 2026 Ofgem price-cap electricity unit rate and standing charge, explains that the cap applies mainly to default tariffs, and notes that some special time-of-use tariffs are excluded. However, it contains no evidence about home-battery prices, battery capacity or efficiency, time-of-use tariff rates, charge/discharge limits, degradation, warranties, or installation economics. It therefore supports tariff and baseline-cost assumptions only, not a complete battery-payback calculation.
findings.evidence: The page states: “The energy price cap for Great Britain is reviewed every three months by Ofgem.” It reports that “Between 1 July to 30 September 2026, annual energy bills for a typical dual-fuel direct debit household in Great Britain are around £1,862,” while warning that this is based on typical usage rather than the homeowner’s actual consumption. Under “What are the current energy price cap rates?” it gives: “Current price cap (July - September 2026)”; “Electricity – daily standing charge 57.19p”; and “Electricity – unit cost per kWh 26.11p.” The page explains that the cap limits “the maximum amount energy suppliers can charge you for each unit of gas or electricity you use” and includes both “the standing charge” and “the price for each unit of electricity and gas you use, measured in pence per kilowatt hours.” It also says that the cap “applies to you if you’re on a default energy tariff” but “doesn’t apply to you if… you’re on a certain type of tariff. For example, some green tariffs and special time of use tariffs.” The page gives Ofgem’s representative electricity consumption as “2,500 kWh” from 1 July 2026, but explicitly says: “This is just a guide. Your actual bills will vary depending on how much energy you use.” For the stated 9,000 kWh annual electricity use, applying the published cap electricity rate alone gives approximately £2,349.90 per year (9,000 × £0.2611), before the annual standing charge of approximately £208.74 (365 × £0.5719), or approximately £2,558.64 including that charge. The household’s stated flat-rate cost of £0.247/kWh is approximately £2,223 per year before standing charges, so the page’s cap rate is about £126.90 per year higher on usage charges; this is not a like-for-like tariff comparison because the existing tariff’s standing charge is not supplied. The page also says the next cap review is due on “26 August 2026” for October–December 2026, demonstrating tariff uncertainty.
findings.summary: The source establishes a useful July 2026 benchmark but does not show that a battery is financially worthwhile. At the published cap rate, a 9,000 kWh household would pay roughly £2,559 annually including the stated electricity standing charge, before considering gas; the homeowner’s current 24.7p/kWh flat rate is cheaper on usage charges, subject to standing-charge differences. A suitable time-of-use tariff could be cheaper than the cap, but the webpage provides no off-peak or peak prices, so savings cannot be calculated from this source. Because the household uses much of its electricity during daytime office hours and can shift little demand, a battery may have limited opportunity to discharge during expensive periods; its economics require actual half-hourly consumption data, a specific tariff, usable capacity, round-trip efficiency, cycling limits, degradation, installation quotation, warranty, and replacement assumptions. No conclusion that either a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery will pay for itself, nor a valid 10-year net outcome or sensitivity analysis, can be supported by this webpage alone.

findings.title: When Is Off-Peak Electricity in the UK? - Jackery UK    – Jackery United Kingdom
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant because it explains UK off-peak and time-of-use electricity periods, describes charging a battery at cheaper times and discharging it during expensive periods, and mentions smart-meter monitoring. However, it is a supplier/manufacturer-affiliated educational page and does not provide the independent, UK-specific financial evidence needed to determine whether a permanently installed 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery would pay for itself for the stated household. In particular, it lacks current installed prices, export/import tariff terms, usable capacity, charge and discharge limits, round-trip efficiency, degradation assumptions, warranties, maintenance, replacement costs, and 10-year cash-flow calculations.
findings.evidence:
Source: “When Is Off-Peak Electricity in the UK? – Jackery UK”, updated 29 April 2026. The page states: “Most consumers pay the same electricity bill regardless of whether they use it during the day or at night. However, an increasing number of consumers are adopting a new type of power billing plan known as time-of-use (TOU). Almost every TOU plan has one thing in common: off-peak electricity is the lowest.” It adds that UK off-peak electricity is “typically available between 10 p.m. and 8 a.m.” and that households can save by shifting electricity use or storing cheaper electricity in a battery and using it during peak periods.

The page explains that peak demand “normally occurs between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.” and that off-peak use is typically “between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m.”, while warning that “your energy company determines the exact dates for peak and off-peak electricity.” Its tariff table says Economy 7 is commonly around midnight to 7 a.m.; EV tariffs are commonly midnight to 5 a.m.; and dynamic smart tariffs are generally cheapest late at night and most expensive from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays. It also says that exact periods vary by “supplier, tariff, and location”.

For battery operation, the page recommends: “If you have a home battery storage system, you can charge during off-peak electricity hours when power prices are low and then use the stored electricity during peak hours to save even more money.” It recommends scheduling high-energy appliances at off-peak times and using a smart meter to “monitor your electricity usage in real-time” and assess whether shifting usage is actually saving money. The page gives a Jackery Explorer 3000 v2 example with a 3,072 Wh battery and claims that charging off-peak and using power during the day can save “up to 15% on your annual electricity bill”; this is a manufacturer claim for a portable power station, not an independent estimate for a UK household battery. It also describes the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus as having 2,042.8 Wh capacity, expandable to 12 kWh, and claims a ten-year life with 70% retained capacity after 4,000 cycles, again without providing a whole-home installed-system cost or independent trial evidence.
findings.summary: The page supports the general mechanism behind battery arbitrage: a smart-meter household may charge at night and discharge during higher-priced periods, with exact periods depending on the tariff. It also supports checking actual half-hourly usage before making a decision. It does not establish that a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery is financially worthwhile, and its “up to 15%” saving statement should not be used as the basis for the requested annual-cost, payback, or 10-year comparison. For the stated home-office household, much daytime electricity may already be consumed during lower or mid-priced periods rather than the 4–8 p.m. peak, reducing the battery’s useful discharge opportunity; some overnight demand would also be consumed directly rather than stored. Independent tariff prices, installed quotations, battery technical data, degradation and replacement assumptions, and the household’s smart-meter half-hourly data are required to calculate the four requested options.

findings.title: Introducing battery-only installation with Octopus | Octopus Energy
findings.rational: The webpage is directly relevant because it addresses battery-only installation without solar panels, identifies the proposed use case—buying electricity during cheap off-peak periods and using it when prices are higher—and gives current indicative installation prices. However, it does not provide the actual time-of-use tariff prices, battery usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, round-trip efficiency, degradation assumptions, warranties, maintenance costs, replacement costs, or export/import rules needed for a reliable 10-year financial assessment. The calculations below therefore separate facts stated by the page from an explicitly illustrative scenario.
findings.evidence:
The page states: “If you’d like battery storage without solar panels ✅ You can take advantage of a battery at home, even without solar panels, by storing energy when it’s cheap, and using it when prices spike.” It adds: “Load up on cheaper, greener energy: store energy from off-peak periods to avoid peak-rate prices with a smart tariff like Agile Octopus.” It also says that Octopus “can install a stand-alone battery for most homes” and that additional storage may be added in future.

Under “What are the benefits of getting a battery?”, the page says: “With battery storage installed at home, you gain the ability to store your own solar power and / or the cheapest and greenest electricity from the grid, by purchasing it at off-peak times. This means you can utilise this free or cheaper energy to power your home, before selling any unused electricity back to the grid at times when prices are higher for a profit.” These are described as potential benefits, not guaranteed savings.

Under “How much does a battery cost?”, the page states: “At present, our prices start at £3,947 for a smart 5kWh battery, £5,336 for an smart 10kWh battery and £7,999 for a 13.5kWh Tesla Powerwall 3 battery.” It says the available products include “the Fox EVO 5 kWh or 10.24 kWh, the Enphase IQ Battery 5P, or the Tesla Powerwall 3,” while also warning that “battery installation is subject to DNO approval” and that an alternative may be offered if the selected product is unsuitable. The page does not state whether the quoted capacities are nominal or usable, nor does it state efficiency, maximum charge/discharge power, degradation, warranty terms, maintenance costs, or replacement assumptions.

Using the household’s stated flat-rate consumption, the no-battery baseline is approximately £1,482 per year at 6,000 kWh, £2,223 per year at 9,000 kWh, and £2,717 per year at 11,000 kWh, before standing charges. The webpage gives no competing flat-rate price or Agile/time-of-use price, so exact costs for options 2–4 cannot be calculated from the source. For illustration only, assume a net peak/off-peak value of £0.15 per kWh after allowing for charging losses, usable capacity equal to the quoted capacity, and 0.5 equivalent full cycles per day rather than assuming a full cycle every day. Indicative annual battery savings would then be about £123 for 5 kWh and £246 for 10 kWh, giving simple paybacks of roughly 32 and 22 years respectively at the quoted £3,947 and £5,336 prices. Over 10 years, ignoring financing, maintenance, degradation and replacement, the battery-only net outcomes would be approximately -£2,715 for 5 kWh and -£2,876 for 10 kWh. Even at one full equivalent cycle per day, the same illustrative spread produces about £246 annual saving for 5 kWh and £493 for 10 kWh: paybacks of roughly 16 and 11 years, before degradation and other costs. A tariff switch without a battery could be worthwhile if daytime consumption can be moved into cheap periods, but this household’s large daytime office demand reduces the amount of load that can be shifted or discharged from an overnight-charged battery during expensive periods.
findings.summary: Based on the webpage alone, a battery-only system is technically feasible but financial payback is unproven. The household’s £2,223 annual flat-rate bill is a useful baseline, but the missing time-of-use prices prevent a definitive comparison. The illustrative calculation suggests that neither a 5 kWh nor a 10 kWh battery is likely to pay for itself within 10 years if usable cycling averages only half a full cycle per day; the 10 kWh option becomes borderline only with an unusually large and persistent tariff spread, close to daily full cycling, low installation cost, and limited degradation. The strongest financial option is likely to test a suitable time-of-use tariff without buying a battery first, because it avoids the £3,947–£5,336 capital cost and the risks of degradation, tariff changes and replacement. The conclusion could change if the household obtains a very high net peak/off-peak spread, can cycle the battery almost every day, receives a substantially lower quotation, or has significant evening/night peak demand rather than predominantly daytime office use. Before deciding, obtain half-hourly smart-meter data for at least 12 months, the exact tariff’s historical and current rates and rules, a battery quote specifying usable kWh, charge/discharge power, round-trip efficiency, warranty and degradation guarantee, DNO/export limitations, maintenance and monitoring costs, and the expected replacement cost. The source does not provide evidence on UK taxes, incentives, VAT treatment, market-rule changes or tariff longevity, so those must be checked separately with Ofgem, HMRC, the supplier and the installer.
