findings.title: Best Energy Deals & Quotes - Cheapest Gas & Electric 2026 | EDF
findings.rational: The most relevant sections are EDF’s descriptions of smart time-of-use tariffs, off-peak charging, battery-specific tariffs, price-cap uncertainty, and its assumptions for solar-and-battery savings. They provide evidence that a smart meter can enable cheaper overnight electricity and that a battery may shift consumption from expensive peak periods, but they do not provide enough information to calculate a reliable battery payback for this household without additional tariff quotations and battery-cost data.
findings.evidence:
EDF states: “Smart time-of-use tariffs offer cheaper electricity at selected times, giving you more control over how and when you use energy. Switching to tariffs such as FreePhase could mean you start saving sooner than you think.”

Under its EV tariffs, EDF says there are “7 hours of cheaper off-peak electricity every night (11 pm-6 am).” Its notes give indicative off-peak rates of “6.49–6.99p/kWh, available for 7 hours between 11 pm and 6 am,” while warning that “Off-peak rates and hours vary by supplier.” Although described as EV tariffs, this is relevant evidence that a smart-meter customer may be able to charge a battery overnight at substantially below the stated current flat rate of approximately 24.7p/kWh.

EDF also describes solar tariffs as follows: “Our import tariffs allow you to save on battery charging with a 10p per kWh overnight discount.” It says customers purchasing new solar panels or batteries from EDF could use the “Empower Fixed Exclusive 12m import tariff,” and that customers with new solar or batteries may earn up to 18p/kWh through a specified SEG export tariff. However, the export-income claims are not directly applicable to a battery-only installation because the household does not expect to install solar panels and would have little or no electricity to export.

EDF explains that variable prices can change: “A variable energy tariff, or plan, means the unit cost of energy can change at any time (often every three months), provided they remain less than or equal to Ofgem’s price cap.” Its notes add that the cap is reviewed in January, April, July and October, and that “Every three months...the price cap level can increase or decrease.” This makes any battery-payback estimate dependent on future peak/off-peak spreads rather than today’s prices alone.

EDF’s battery example is explicitly solar-based. It says a typical household with 2,500 kWh of solar generation and a 3 kWh battery could pay £0 under specified July 2026 import and export tariffs, assuming solar is prioritised for home use, excess is stored, the battery discharges during peak hours, and the battery is topped up from imported energy overnight. This example should not be transferred to the stated battery-only household: it relies on solar generation and export revenue, and does not establish the installed price, usable capacity, round-trip efficiency, degradation, maximum charge/discharge rate, warranty, or replacement cost of a battery.
findings.summary: The page supports switching to a suitable time-of-use tariff without a battery as the lowest-risk option: the household could directly use cheap overnight electricity for any flexible loads, although its unusually high daytime office demand limits the benefit. A battery could also buy overnight electricity and discharge during peak periods, but the page supplies no battery price or technical data and gives no battery-only payback calculation. Using the supplied household flat rate of 24.7p/kWh and EDF’s indicative 6.49–6.99p/kWh overnight rate, the gross energy-price spread is about 17.7–18.2p/kWh before standing charges, charging losses, battery degradation and tariff changes. A 5 kWh battery therefore cannot be assumed to cycle fully every day; its economics depend on how much daytime demand occurs during the tariff’s peak period, whether overnight electricity is consumed directly, usable rather than nominal capacity, and the installed quotation. The strongest evidence-based conclusion from this page is that tariff switching may provide meaningful savings, whereas neither a 5 kWh nor 10 kWh battery can be judged worthwhile from EDF’s claims alone. The homeowner should obtain half-hourly smart-meter data, exact time-of-use rates and hours, standing charges, export/import conditions, and several installed battery quotations specifying usable capacity, continuous and peak charge/discharge power, round-trip efficiency, degradation or throughput warranty, outage functionality, maintenance, VAT treatment, and replacement terms.

findings.title: Smart Export Guarantee & Tariff | Solar Energy | EDF
findings.rational: The webpage is relevant mainly because it states EDF’s current export-tariff rates and eligibility rules for battery owners. It does not provide the import time-of-use rates, battery purchase and installation prices, usable capacity, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, degradation, warranty, or maintenance assumptions needed to determine whether a battery without solar would pay for itself. Consequently, it can inform the value of exporting electricity but cannot by itself support the requested 5 kWh versus 10 kWh financial comparison.
findings.evidence:
EDF states: “Our best SEG tariffs… Submit your enquiry and purchase after 2 March 2026 to qualify… Export Exclusive 12m V3… Get this offer with solar, a battery, or both – T&Cs apply. Have your MCS or Flexi Orb certificate ready if buying a battery only… Get paid 18p per kWh for the energy you export… Switch or leave anytime - this tariff has no exit fees.” The same section lists “Export 12m… 15p per kWh for the energy you export… 1-year fixed tariff… No exit fees.” EDF also says that its variable export tariffs pay “5.6p per kWh” for EDF customers or “3.0p per kWh” for anyone, with the warning that the export price “may go up or down.” [EDF, Smart Export Guarantee & Tariff | Solar Energy]

EDF explains the eligibility limitation: “The Smart Export Guarantee (SEG) is a licensee requirement to offer an export tariff to eligible generators.” Eligible technologies are “solar photovoltaic (solar PV), wind, micro combined heat and power (CHP), hydro, anaerobic digestion (AD).” Customers need “a smart meter or half-hourly electricity meter.” In the FAQ, EDF states: “If there is an eligible renewable energy installation linked to the battery storage, any electricity fed into the grid will be eligible for SEG payments.” Its requirements also say the installation must consist of “Anaerobic Digestion, PV, onshore wind and/or Hydro generation only,” while the Export Exclusive and fixed tariffs are described as “only available for solar PV.” Therefore, a battery-only household must verify the precise MCS/Flexi-Orb and tariff terms; a battery charging from the grid is not, by itself, renewable generation eligible for SEG.

EDF’s savings example is not applicable to the proposed no-solar household. The page says: “Savings based on July 2026 Standard Variable Price Cap and dependent on household consumption patterns.” It describes a typical household with “2,500 kWh of solar generation and a battery with a capacity of 3kWh” paying £0 under an import/export tariff, assuming solar powers the home, excess is stored, the battery discharges during peak hours, and it is topped up using imported energy overnight. This example assumes solar generation and therefore cannot be used as evidence that a 5 kWh or 10 kWh battery without solar will achieve the same result. The page provides no battery-only installation price, import tariff schedule, round-trip efficiency, degradation rate, replacement cost, or charge/discharge power rating.
findings.summary: The strongest relevant finding is that EDF advertises post-2 March 2026 export rates of 18p/kWh, 15p/kWh, 5.6p/kWh, or 3.0p/kWh, but SEG payments concern eligible renewable generation and are not a substitute for an import time-of-use tariff. The page does not establish that a grid-charged battery without solar can receive SEG payments, except that EDF says battery-only applicants for one tariff should provide an MCS or Flexi-Orb certificate and comply with its terms. Because the household has no solar and the source supplies neither off-peak/peak import prices nor battery economics, no defensible annual cost, payback, sensitivity analysis, or 10-year outcome can be calculated from this webpage alone. The homeowner should obtain the exact battery-only tariff terms, half-hourly import rates, export eligibility confirmation, and independent installed quotations before deciding.
